newsitem.title: KUWAIT: MP shooting spurs parliament anti-corruption effort.
newsitem.headline: MP shooting spurs parliament anti-corruption effort.

text.p: An attempt to kill a leading Kuwaiti opposition MP has provided parliament a new momentum and public support to combat alleged corruption, analysts said on Wednesday.

Parliament's new found strength is expected to unite various political groupings to reopen old probes and launch new ones into alleged corruption and -- backed by a strong public opinion -- reiterate demands for clear government action against what some MPs call "public funds thieves", they said.
Many analysts had expected the parliament, elected in October 1996, to be less confrontational than one formed just after the Gulf War.
But Friday's shooting of Abdullah al-Naibari has given parliament "a new direction," according to one diplomat.

"It was seen as floating around a bit. Now it has this common direction which every political group can dig its teeth into," the diplomat said. "MPs are holding the government responsible for the alleged corruption".
Three Kuwaiti and two Iranian suspects have been arrested in connection with the attack on the Oxford-educated Naibari, who is recovering from the shooting.
No charges have been filed, but some MPs allege lack of firm government action against former officials who allegedly made illegal profits and squandered public funds led to the attack.

The government has responded with a veiled threat to dissolve the only elected Gulf Arab house, while some politicians say the cabinet must go. Parliament was dissolved in 1986 but it was restored in 1992 in line with a promise made during Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait.

"Do not make me lose by temper and be forced to take action in something that we all don't like," acting premier and Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah told parliament on Tuesday in what many saw as a warning to dissolve the house.

A Kuwaiti analyst said any move to dissolve parliament would be received with "great public displeasure," adding: "The people, not just MPs, demand to know the truth about the assassination and the corruption charges."
Said a Western diplomat: "Things have changed since the Gulf War. Parliament has its own identity now and the people will react strongly against a move to dissolve it."
Calls by the state for national unity are not working, the diplomat said. "Parliament now has a new dynamic and public support after a period of perceived weakness," he added.

The weekly Talea of Naibari's political group on Wednesday launched fresh attacks, claiming that "corruption has become institutionalised with its own organisation, powers, media...and its penetrations of official and security apparatuses."
Some prominent politicians have also voiced doubts that the assassination attempt investigation would be impartial.

Naibari's longtime political partner, prominent former MP Ahmad al-Khateeb, charged: "The case is not in safe hands and we have the right to worry. I am not stupid. I know what is going on in this country. There is a hidden government that is ruling."

But Sheikh Sabah had responded angrily to such comments, telling reporters after a stormy parliament session: "I will not accept to be accused of protecting a criminal or a thief." He said that no one, including himself, was above the law.
